source: Ordinary graphic-design and advertising art-direction practice - type hierarchy, the thirds grid, logo lockups and reading order. NOT AI Video Bootcamp course material; the same honesty convention tools/capture_bank.json, tools/style_bank.json's `tilt-shift` entry and tools/macro_insert_bank.json already use. What prompted it: a repo-wide grep for typography, headline, logo, copy placement, kerning, lockup, typeface or type hierarchy across every bank and tool returned NOTHING about text inside an image - the only hits were ui/tokens.py's own Qt stylesheet fonts and one photographic phrase, `negative-space`. `\blogo\b` had zero hits in tools/ entirely. So an app that builds advertising could describe the photograph and not one word of the advert laid over it.
note:
This is the first vocabulary in this app for text INSIDE an image, as opposed to tools/build_social.py's caption copy, which is text ABOUT a post. Every phrase declares the realism_lint layer it strengthens and tools/typography_lint.py checks per phrase that the layer can actually SEE it - a phrase the gate cannot detect is decoration, which is exactly what tools/story_bank.json's four fur phrases turned out to be.

Most phrases land on `composition`, and that is not a fudge: reserving an even-toned region of the frame for type IS a compositional instruction, and it is the one that decides whether the type ends up legible. A zone phrase therefore does two jobs at once - it tells the layout where the words go, and it tells the photograph to keep that area quiet.

WHY `dominance` AND `ratio` ARE CHECKED AGAINST EACH OTHER. The commonest way a layout dies is that everything is loud, so nothing leads. That is hard to detect from words alone - but a contradiction between the two decisions that express it is not. Saying the type leads while allotting it a tenth of the frame is a flat hierarchy stated in two places, and compose_typography() refuses it by name. This is the same shape tools/build_color.py uses when it refuses --mood and --film-look together: two complete recipes that cannot both win.

WORD COUNTS ARE A REAL CONSTRAINT, NOT STYLE ADVICE. Image models garble long strings: a three-word headline renders cleanly far more often than a twelve-word one, and legal lines never render legibly at all. Each ratio therefore carries `max_words`, and the bank says plainly that anything longer belongs in a typesetting tool over a clean plate rather than in the generation prompt.

dominance.label: What leads
dominance.note: The single most important decision in the layout: which element the eye is required to hit first. Exactly one - that is what makes it a hierarchy rather than a pile.

image-led.label: The image leads
image-led.phrase: the photograph carries the frame with the type kept small and subordinate, a clear visual hierarchy with one dominant element
image-led.note: The default for brand and lifestyle work. The picture does the selling; the words name the brand and get out.

product-led.label: The product leads
product-led.phrase: the product dominating the frame as the single focal point, type kept subordinate to it, a clear visual hierarchy
product-led.note: Pack shots and launches. The product is the hero and the type must not compete with it.

type-led.label: The type leads
type-led.phrase: the headline dominating the frame as the primary element, the photograph supporting it, a clear visual hierarchy with one dominant element
type-led.note: Statement and campaign posters. Only works when the line is genuinely worth the space.

ratio.label: Type-to-image ratio
ratio.note: How much of the frame the words are allowed. Carries `max_words`, because an image model garbles long strings and a headline that will not render is not a headline.

whisper.label: 10/90 - a whisper
whisper.phrase: type occupying roughly a tenth of the frame, the rest given to the photograph
whisper.note: A brand name and nothing else. The most reliable ratio to generate, because there is almost nothing to render.

editorial.label: 20/80 - editorial
editorial.phrase: type occupying roughly a fifth of the frame in a single block, the rest given to the photograph
editorial.note: A short headline plus a lockup. The usual answer for a social ad.

poster.label: 40/60 - poster
poster.phrase: type occupying roughly two fifths of the frame as a deliberate typographic block, the photograph filling the remainder
poster.note: The words are half the idea. Expect to fix the rendering by hand more often.

type-first.label: 60/40 - type first
type-first.phrase: a dominant typographic block across the majority of the frame with the photograph as a supporting field behind it
type-first.note: A statement poster. At this size, seriously consider typesetting over a clean plate instead.

zone.label: Type zone
zone.note: Where the words sit, on a thirds grid - and, in the same breath, an instruction to keep that region of the PHOTOGRAPH quiet. Type over busy detail is illegible no matter how it is set.

upper-left.label: Upper-left third
upper-left.phrase: generous negative space reserved for type across the upper-left third, that area kept even-toned and uncluttered
upper-left.note: Where a Western eye enters the frame. The safest default.

upper-band.label: Upper band
upper-band.phrase: generous negative space reserved for type across the upper third as a full-width band, that area kept even-toned and uncluttered
upper-band.note: A headline running the width of the frame above the subject.

lower-band.label: Lower band
lower-band.phrase: generous negative space reserved for type across the lower third as a full-width band, that area kept even-toned and uncluttered
lower-band.note: Pairs with a subject looking up or out of the top of the frame.

centre.label: Centred
centre.phrase: generous negative space reserved for type through the centre of the frame, that area kept even-toned and uncluttered
centre.note: Demands a symmetrical or empty middle. Fights most portraits.

side-column.label: Side column
side-column.phrase: generous negative space reserved for type as a vertical column down one side, that area kept even-toned and uncluttered
side-column.note: For a subject pushed hard to one side, with lead room the type then occupies.

lockup.label: Logo lockup
lockup.note: Where the brand mark sits and how big it is. Scale is stated as a fraction of the frame, because 'small' is not an instruction.

corner-quiet.label: Bottom-right, quiet
corner-quiet.phrase: a small brand logo lockup in the bottom-right corner, about an eighth of the frame width
corner-quiet.note: The default. Present, legible, not competing.

under-headline.label: Centred under the headline
under-headline.phrase: a brand logo lockup centred directly beneath the headline, about a sixth of the frame width
under-headline.note: Ties the mark to the line. Needs the headline to be centred too.

top-left.label: Top-left, masthead
top-left.phrase: a small brand logo lockup in the top-left corner, about an eighth of the frame width
top-left.note: Reads as a masthead. Do not combine with an upper-left type zone.

none.label: No logo in frame
none.restraint_note: The only binary option in this bank. Its siblings all state a magnitude - small, about an eighth of the frame width - and the hedging check is right to demand one of them. There either is a lockup or there is not, so there is no intensity here to hedge. A group-level flag would have exempted the three placements too, which do need it.
none.phrase: the packaging itself carrying the brand mark, with no separate logo lockup added
none.note: A real answer, and often the right one when the pack is already in shot.

reading_order.label: Reading order
reading_order.note: The path the eye is asked to take, stated explicitly. Left unstated it is decided by accident.

headline-product-logo.label: Headline, product, logo
headline-product-logo.phrase: a deliberate reading order leading the eye from the headline to the product and then to the logo
headline-product-logo.note: The standard for a claim-led ad.

image-headline-logo.label: Image, headline, logo
image-headline-logo.phrase: a deliberate reading order leading the eye from the photograph to the headline and then to the logo
image-headline-logo.note: For when the picture is the hook and the line is the payoff.

product-headline.label: Product, then headline
product-headline.phrase: a deliberate reading order leading the eye to the product first and then to the headline beside it
product-headline.note: Launches, where recognising the pack is the whole job.

restraint.label: Copy restraint
restraint.note: The discipline that keeps a layout readable. Stated positively, because realism_lint.is_negated() suppresses a layer key sitting inside a negation - correctly, since a prompt should not score for what it is ruling out. Two options here were written the wrong way round at first (leading with no brand logo in the frame, and with no small print or legal line) and were invisible to the gate as a result. Both now lead with the positive half - the packaging itself carrying the brand mark, and the type limited to what reads at a glance - keeping the negative as a trailing clause, which is the same shape prompt_bank.json's own 'authentic pores visible, not airbrushed smooth' already uses.

one-idea.label: One idea per frame
one-idea.phrase: one idea per frame, a single headline with no competing subhead

no-legal.label: No small print
no-legal.phrase: the type limited to what reads at a glance, no small print or legal line
no-legal.note: Legal copy never renders legibly. Add it later over a clean plate.

type-clear-of-subject.label: Type clear of the subject
type-clear-of-subject.phrase: the type kept clear of the subject's face and of the product label, overlapping neither
type-clear-of-subject.note: The single commonest way a generated ad is ruined.

compatibility.note: Which dominance each ratio can honestly express. A layout that says the type leads while giving it a tenth of the frame is a flat hierarchy stated twice, and compose_typography() refuses it by name rather than quietly picking one. Keyed by dominance; the value is the ratios that agree with it.

conflicts.note: Pairs that are individually fine and together are not. Checked by name, not inferred - `top-left` puts the mark exactly where `upper-left` puts the headline, and the two would be set on top of each other.
